endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: To protect patient privacy and ensure consumer confidence, healthcare organizations must ensure the data privacy and the transparency of AI use to patients and staff.

endorsements.title: Action Guide: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
endorsements.issuer: National Association of Community Health Centers
endorsements.quote: Dependence on AI recommendations carries risks - clinicians must cross-check results and maintain transparency by informing patients when AI is being used.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Determine whether there is an accessible, easy-tounderstand way for affected groups to know that part of their treatment was determined by an AI solution

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Most AI-enabled workflows require transparency (i.e., clear, accessible disclosure of how AI may inform care) and do not require formal patient consent.

endorsements.title: Texas SB 1188 (89th Legislature), electronic health records and AI disclosure
endorsements.quote: A health care practitioner who uses artificial intelligence for diagnostic purposes as described by Subsection (a) must disclose the practitioner's use of that technology to the practitioner's patients.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Health care AI must be designed, developed, and deployed in a manner which is ethical, equitable, responsible, accurate, transparent, and evidence-based.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: The concept of transparency should also extend to patients being made aware if AI systems are being used.

endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: Texas has adopted parallel transparency requirements: SB 1188 mandates that practitioners disclose the use of AI for diagnostic purposes to patients15, while HB 149 (the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act) requires disclosure when consumers interact with AI systems, including in healthcare service contexts16.

endorsements.title: Commentary: Patient Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence; What have We Learned and How Should We Move Forward?

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations of Using ChatGPT in Health Care

endorsements.title: Establishing a Multi-Society Generative AI Task Force Within Radiology

endorsements.title: Implications of Large Language Models for Clinical Practice: Ethical Analysis Through the Principlism Framework
endorsements.issuer: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
endorsements.quote: In the context of LLMs in clinical practice, this requires the patient to be informed that LLMs might be used by the medical practitioners that are providing patient care, such that the consent that the patient provides to receive that care can be adequately informed (the WHO 2021 guidance states that ‘the use of machine‐learning algorithms [such as LLMs] in diagnosis, prognosis and treatment plans should be incorporated into the process for informed and valid consent’) [ 31 ].

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence and science of patient input: a perspective from people with multiple sclerosis
endorsements.quote: To enhance trust, people should be made aware when AI or algorithms are being used in decision-making relating to their healthcare.

endorsements.title: Expert consensus on feasibility and application of automatic pain assessment in routine clinical use
endorsements.issuer: Journal of anesthesia, analgesia and critical care
endorsements.quote: The patient must be aware of the use of AI techniques (for diagnostic and/or therapeutic purposes) and their application limitations (e.g., accuracy not 100%) and must be provided with documentation/clinical explanations

endorsements.issuer: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open

endorsements.title: Medicine, healthcare and the AI act: gaps, challenges and future implications
endorsements.quote: Transparency also extends to informing patients when AI is used in their care, promoting trust and informed consent.

endorsements.title: Harm Reduction Strategies for Thoughtful Use of Large Language Models in the Medical Domain: Perspectives for Patients and Clinicians

endorsements.title: Patient Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging

endorsements.title: The Ethical Boundaries of Chairside Generative Artificial Intelligence in Dental Education

endorsements.title: Practical consequences of the European union-AI act for anatomic pathology laboratories a European society of pathology and European society of digital and integrative pathology commissioned expert opinion paper
endorsements.issuer: Virchows Archiv : an international journal of pathology

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in medicine: a position paper by the Italian Society of Internal Medicine

endorsements.title: Legal, ethical, and policy challenges of artificial intelligence translation tools in healthcare

endorsements.title: From Agents to Governance: Essential AI Skills for Clinicians in the Large Language Model Era
endorsements.quote: Clinicians should disclose when AI is used (eg, AI-scribed summaries, patient-portal messages, and patient education materials) to uphold patient autonomy and informed consent [ 26 ].

endorsements.title: Asia-Pacific consensus on the use of artificial intelligence in colorectal cancer screening and surveillance
endorsements.quote: Statement 10. Patient should be informed when AI-assisted colonoscopy is used in CRC screening.

endorsements.title: Equity at the point of care: auditing AI-supported resource allocation in obstetric emergencies

endorsements.title: A testable framework linking diagnostic AI contribution to outcome measurement in clinical decision support

endorsements.title: Principles for Responsible AI in Health Professions Education, Research, and Care: Health CARE-AI (Contextual, Accountable, Responsible, and Equitable Artificial Intelligence) Framework Delphi Consensus Study

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in psychiatry: clinical applications, limitations, and ethical challenges

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in the EU Safe Hearts Plan: prediction alone is not enough

evidence.title: Receiving information on machine learning-based clinical decision support systems in psychiatric services may increase patient trust in these systems: A randomised survey experiment
evidence.effect: Mean absolute difference in trust: 5% [95%CI: 1%;9%], p-value= 0·009 vs active; 4% [1%;8%], p-value=0·015 vs blank.
evidence.quote: The intervention increased trust in ML-based clinical decision support systems when compared to the active control (mean absolute difference in trust: 5% [95%CI: 1%;9%], p-value= 0·009) and the blank control arm (mean absolute difference in trust: 4% [1%;8%], p-value=0·015).

evidence.title: Patient perspectives on informed consent for medical AI: A web-based experiment
evidence.outcome: Perceived importance of AI-use information vs. radiologist consultation and standard surgery information
evidence.effect: AI use raised perceived importance of nearly all information items vs radiologist (e.g., 'AI used' mean diff -.2863, p<0.001); AI information rated more important than or similar to short-term effect information.
evidence.quote: This result provides support for a disclosure of information regarding AI use when AI is used in diagnosis.

evidence.title: Patient Reactions to Artificial Intelligence-Clinician Discrepancies: Web-Based Randomized Experiment
evidence.outcome: Patient agreement with and ratings of radiologist when AI involvement is disclosed versus no AI
evidence.effect: Agreement was lower only when the radiologist undercalled AI (mean 4.01) versus overcalled AI (4.63), agreed with AI (4.55), or had no AI (4.57). Disclosed AI agreement caused no penalty; undercalling lowered recommendation and ratings.
evidence.quote: Participants' agreement with the radiologist's recommendation was significantly lower when the radiologist undercalled AI (mean 4.01, SE 0.07, P<.001) than in the other 3 conditions, with no significant differences among them (radiologist overcalled AI [mean 4.63, SE 0.06], agreed with AI [mean 4.55, SE 0.07], or had no AI [mean 4.57, SE 0.06]).

evidence.title: Should AI results be disclosed in mammography reports? A randomised survey study of patient responses to concordant and discordant interpretations
evidence.outcome: trust, anxiety, second-opinion and legal intent
evidence.effect: Discordant AI disclosure: trust 73.0 vs 90.1; anxiety 58.0% vs 16.0%; second-opinion 50.0% vs 8.7%; legal action 60.7% vs 38.7%.
evidence.quote: Disclosure of a discordant AI result significantly reduced trust in the radiologist (73.0 vs 90.1; p < 0.001), and increased anxiety (58.0% vs 16.0%; OR = 15.4), second-opinion intent (50.0% vs 8.7%; OR = 10.2), and legal action consideration (60.7% vs 38.7%; OR = 2.49).

evidence.title: Acceptability of AI-Assisted Psychotherapy to Prospective Patients and Their Intent to Continue Treatment: A Vignette Study
evidence.outcome: Acceptability and continuation intent under transparent vs covert therapist AI use
evidence.effect: Covert AI use produced the strongest declines in acceptability and continuation intent; transparency reduced but did not eliminate negative reactions (all p<0.001 vs control).
evidence.quote: Transparency reduced, but did not eliminate, negative reactions.

evidence.title: Me, my doctor and AI: a qualitative interview study on patients' requirements for trustworthy use of AI-CDSS in ophthalmology
evidence.outcome: Patient expectations of being informed when AI-CDSS contributes to their care
evidence.effect: Almost all participants expected to be informed when AI-CDSS were used; preferences on the amount and format of information varied.
evidence.quote: Almost all participants expected to be informed when AI-CDSS were used, although preferences regarding the amount and format of information varied.

evidence.title: AI Implementation in Safety Net Healthcare: Understanding Barriers and Strategies
evidence.outcome: Barriers in communicating with patients about AI use
evidence.effect: Limited guidance on communicating with patients about AI use was a key barrier for the safety net organizations. No numeric results reported.
evidence.quote: Key barriers emerged during the Integration and Lifecycle Management phases and included gaps in AI performance evaluation and impact assessments, communication with patients about AI use, foundational AI education, financial resources for purchasing and maintaining AI tools, and AI governance structures.

evidence.title: Awareness of Racial and Ethnic Bias and Potential Solutions to Address Bias With Use of Health Care Algorithms
evidence.outcome: Clinician and patient awareness of algorithm use and potential for bias
evidence.effect: Theme 3: clinicians and patients are often unaware of the use of algorithms and potential for bias.
evidence.quote: The 7 qualitative themes, with 31 subthemes, included the following: (1) algorithms are in widespread use and have significant repercussions, (2) bias can result from algorithms whether or not they explicitly include race, (3) clinicians and patients are often unaware of the use of algorithms and potential for bias, (4) race is a social construct used as a proxy for clinical variables, (5) there is a lack of standardization in how race and social determinants of health are collected and defined, (6) bias can be introduced at all stages of algorithm development, and (7) algorithms should be discussed as part of shared decision-making between the patient and clinician.
evidence.sample_unit: respondents to request for information (organization representatives and individuals)

evidence.title: Patient Preferences for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging: A Single-Center Cross-Sectional Survey
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: Patient preference for being informed of AI use in their imaging care, and self-rated AI knowledge
evidence.effect: 90.3% (204/226) believed they should be informed about AI use in their care; 67.4% (151/224) reported minimal to no AI knowledge. Authors note a discrepancy between patient preferences and current clinical practice.
evidence.quote: 90.3% (204/226) believed they should be informed about the use of AI in their care, and 91.1% (204/224) supported the right to opt out.
evidence.sample_unit: patients undergoing outpatient CT or MRI

evidence.title: Informed Consent Disclosures and Minimum Requirements in AI Clinical Trials: Cross-Sectional Analysis
evidence.outcome: Disclosure of AI type or intended use in consent documents
evidence.effect: 66/114 (58%) of ICs failed to disclose the AI type or its intended use; 18.4% (n=21) omitted risks entirely.
evidence.quote: More than half (66/114, 58%) of ICs failed to disclose the AI type or its intended use, and 18.4% (n=21) omitted risks entirely.
evidence.sample_unit: informed consent documents from AI clinical trials

commentary.bottom_line: Forty-two sources endorse telling patients when AI contributes to their care, and six simulated studies suggest disclosure may modestly raise or preserve trust, although one study found that disclosing AI that disagreed with the clinician raised anxiety and second-opinion intent. No study has tested disclosure in routine care or measured its effect on patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Six studies test disclosure, and all used simulated or offline settings with trust, acceptability, or intent as outcomes rather than care outcomes. Two randomized trials found a 5% trust difference in Denmark and no agreement penalty for disclosed AI in the United States. An Italian vignette study found harms when AI and clinician disagreed, so results are inconsistent and indirect.

In the Italian mammography vignette, disclosing AI that disagreed with the clinician lowered trust from 90.1 to 73.0, raised anxiety from 16.0% to 58.0%, and raised second-opinion intent from 8.7% to 50.0%. In a US trial, agreement fell to 4.01 when the radiologist undercalled AI. Disclosure may change how patients respond to discordant findings.

Almost all German ophthalmology patients interviewed expected to be told about AI decision support, but they differed on how much information they wanted and in what format. Among 226 imaging patients, 67.4% reported minimal or no AI knowledge. No study tested a disclosure script or workflow in routine care, so fidelity and clinician burden remain unmeasured.

No test of disclosure enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A qualitative study of five US safety-net organizations found that limited guidance on communicating with patients about AI was a key barrier. A request-for-information analysis found that clinicians and patients are often unaware of algorithm use and its potential for bias.

Texas SB 1188 requires practitioners who use AI for diagnostic purposes to disclose it to patients, and HB 149 requires disclosure when consumers interact with AI. Among 114 consent documents from AI clinical trials, 58% did not disclose the AI type or intended use and 18.4% omitted risks. These findings show a disclosure gap, not the effect of closing it.

No study reported the staff time, cost, or training needed to disclose AI use at scale. The safety-net study identified missing communication guidance as a barrier, which suggests that systems adopting this practice may need to develop their own scripts and patient materials.

In a survey of 226 imaging patients, 90.3% believed they should be informed about AI use. In a US vignette study of 201 adults, covert AI use in therapy produced the largest declines in acceptability and continuation intent, and transparency reduced but did not remove negative reactions. A Korean survey of 1,000 respondents rated AI-use information as important.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested AI disclosure in a live clinical deployment. A pragmatic trial comparing disclosure formats in routine care would need to measure patient comprehension, trust, second-opinion seeking, and downstream care decisions, with particular attention to how clinicians explain cases where AI output and clinical judgment disagree.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the six tests of disclosure included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only safety-net evidence is a hazard study reporting that organizations lacked guidance on how to talk with patients about AI, and with 67.4% of imaging patients reporting minimal AI knowledge, the effect of disclosure on comprehension and trust in these groups is unknown.
